I had therefore read those urgent and repeated letters, and I had torn them up without telling Marguerite what they contained, and without advising her to see the old man again, although a feeling of pity for the poor man's grief inclined me to do so; but I feared that in this advice she might see a desire, by having the duke resume his former visits, to make him resume the expenses of the household; above all, I dreaded that she might think me capable of denying responsibility for her life in all the consequences into which her love for me might lead her.

The result was that the duke, receiving no reply, ceased writing, and that Marguerite and I continued to live together without concerning ourselves with the future.




Chapter XVIII


It would be difficult to give you details of our new life. It consisted of a series of childish pastimes that were delightful to us, but insignificant to those to whom I might recount them.

You know what it is to love a woman; you know how the days grow shorter, and with what amorous indolence one lets oneself be carried into the morrow. You are familiar with that forgetfulness of all things which springs from a violent, trusting, and reciprocated love. Every being who is not the beloved woman seems a useless being in creation. One regrets having already cast fragments of one's heart to other women, and one cannot conceive the possibility of ever clasping any hand other than the one one holds in one's own. The mind admits neither work nor memory, nothing, in short, that might distract it from the one thought constantly offered to it. Every day one discovers in one's mistress a new charm, an unknown delight. Existence is nothing more than the repeated fulfillment of a continuous desire; the soul is nothing more than the vestal charged with tending the sacred fire of love.

Often, when night had fallen, we would go and sit beneath the little wood overlooking the house. There we listened to the cheerful harmonies of the evening, both thinking of the approaching hour that would leave us in each other's arms until the next day. At other times we remained in bed all day, without even letting the sun enter our room. The curtains were tightly closed, and the outside world stopped for a while for us. Nanine alone had the right to open our door, but only to bring us our meals; and even those we ate without getting up, constantly interrupting them with laughter and wild antics. This was followed by a few moments' sleep, for, vanishing into our love, we were like two persistent divers who return to the surface only to draw breath.

Nevertheless, I caught moments of sadness, and sometimes even tears, in Marguerite; I asked her where this sudden sorrow came from, and she would reply:

“Our love is not an ordinary love, my dear Armand. You love me as though I had never belonged to anyone, and I tremble lest later, repenting of your love and holding my past against me as a crime, you force me to cast myself back into the life in the midst of which you found me. Remember that now that I have tasted a new life, I would die if I returned to the other one. Tell me, then, that you will never leave me.”

“I swear it to you!”

At these words, she would look at me as though to read in my eyes whether my oath was sincere; then she would throw herself into my arms and, hiding her head against my breast, say to me:

“It is because you do not know how much I love you!”

One evening, we were leaning on the window balcony; we were watching the moon, which seemed to be emerging with difficulty from its bed of clouds, and listening to the wind noisily stirring the trees. We were holding hands and had not spoken for a good quarter of an hour when Marguerite said to me:

“Winter is here; would you like us to leave?”

“And for where?”

“For Italy.”

“Are you bored, then?”

“I am afraid of winter; above all, I am afraid of our return to Paris.”

“Why?”

“For many reasons.”

And she abruptly went on, without giving me the reasons for her fears:

“Will you leave? I will sell everything I have; we will go and live over there; nothing will remain to me of what I was; no one will know who I am. Will you do it?”

“Let us leave, if that would please you, Marguerite; let us take a journey,” I said to her; “but what need is there to sell things you will be glad to find upon our return? I do not have a large enough fortune to accept such a sacrifice, but I have enough for us to travel in fine style for five or six months, if that appeals to you in the slightest.”

“Actually, no,” she continued, leaving the window and going to sit on the sofa in the shadow of the room; “what is the use of going to spend money over there? I already cost you quite enough here.”

“You reproach me with it, Marguerite; that is not generous.”

“Forgive me, my friend,” she said, holding out her hand to me; “this stormy weather is bad for my nerves; I do not say what I mean to say.”

And, after kissing me, she fell into a long reverie.

Similar scenes took place several times, and although I did not know what gave rise to them, I nonetheless perceived in Marguerite a feeling of anxiety about the future. She could not doubt my love, for it grew each day, and yet I often saw her sad without her ever explaining the cause of her sadness to me except by attributing it to a physical cause.

Fearing that she might grow weary of a life that was too monotonous, I suggested that she return to Paris, but she always rejected this suggestion and assured me that she could not be as happy anywhere as she was in the country.

Prudence now came only rarely, but in return she wrote letters that I had never asked to see, although each time they plunged Marguerite into deep preoccupation. I did not know what to think.

One day Marguerite remained in her room.

I entered. She was writing.

“To whom are you writing?” I asked her.

“To Prudence. Would you like me to read you what I am writing?”

I abhorred anything that might appear to be suspicion, so I replied to Marguerite that I had no need to know what she was writing; and yet, I was certain of it, that letter would have revealed to me the true cause of her sadness.

The next day the weather was splendid. Marguerite suggested that we go for a boat ride and visit the island of Croissy. She seemed very cheerful; it was five o'clock when we returned.
